n: The Lord speaks again to Moses. This chapter is one of the richest in Leviticus, showing that holiness touches every part of daily life.
The theme of the whole book: be holy because God is holy. Holiness means being set apart for God and becoming like Him. Peter quotes this verse.

f.g: Hebrew qadosh—set apart, distinct, belonging to God.

n: Respecting parents and keeping the Sabbath come first—echoing the Ten Commandments. Interestingly, mother is named before father here.

f.g: Here, to revere or deeply respect.

n: No idols or cast-metal gods. Worship belongs to the living God alone.

f.g: Idols made by pouring melted metal into molds.

n: Peace offerings are to be given willingly, in a way God accepts.

f.g: Voluntarily, so that it will be accepted for you.

n: The meat must be eaten within two days; leftovers on the third day are burned.

f.g: ought = anything

n: Eating it on the third day makes it unacceptable—sacred things have limits.
Doing so treats holy things carelessly, which brings guilt and being cut off.

f.g: Treated a sacred thing as ordinary.

n: Farmers must not harvest the edges of their fields or pick up what falls. The leftovers belong to the poor—a built-in welfare system.

f.g: Grain left behind by harvesters, which the poor could gather.

n: Vineyards too must not be stripped bare; some grapes are left for the poor and foreigners. Generosity was part of holiness.
No stealing, cheating, or lying—honesty in all dealings.
Swearing falsely by God’s name dishonors Him. Using His name to back up a lie was especially serious.
No defrauding or robbing. Day laborers must be paid the same day, since they depended on that wage to eat.

f.w: the wages of him that is hired

n: Do not take advantage of those who cannot hear or see. God sees what the deaf cannot hear and the blind cannot see, so “fear thy God.”

f.g: Something placed to make a person trip.

n: Judges must be fair—not favoring the poor out of pity or the powerful out of fear. True justice is impartial.

f.g: Show favoritism.

n: No gossiping or spreading slander, and no standing idly by when a neighbor’s life is in danger.

f.g: A gossip or slanderer.

f.w: stand against the blood of thy neighbour
f.g: Endanger your neighbor’s life, or stand by while it is threatened.

n: Do not secretly hate others. Instead, speak to them honestly about a wrong so resentment does not grow and you do not share in their sin.

f.g: By all means.

n: “Love thy neighbour as thyself”—Jesus called this the second great commandment. Holiness rules out revenge and grudges.
No mixing of animal breeds, seed types, or linen with wool. These rules likely taught Israel to respect God’s created order and to stay distinct.

f.g: gender = breed
A different species.

n: If a man sleeps with a slave woman engaged to another man, there is punishment but not death, since she was not free to refuse. The law recognized her vulnerable status.

f.g: A female servant or slave.
Here probably means an inquiry or punishment; the Hebrew is uncertain.

n: The man must bring a ram as a guilt offering.
Through the offering he can be forgiven. The law offered a way back even after serious wrong.
Newly planted fruit trees are not harvested for three years—treated as “uncircumcised,” not yet dedicated. This also let trees mature.

f.g: Here meaning forbidden, not yet consecrated.

n: In the fourth year all the fruit is holy, given in thanks to God—a kind of firstfruits.

f.g: withal = with it

n: From the fifth year on, the owner may eat. Giving God the first brought the promise of greater increase.
No eating blood, and no fortune-telling or reading omens. Israel was to trust God rather than occult practices.

f.g: Divination, magic.
Look for good or bad omens; practice soothsaying.

n: No trimming hair or beards in certain styles—probably practices tied to pagan mourning or worship.

f.w: round the corners of your heads
f.g: Cut the hair at the temples, as some pagan rites did.
mar = damage, spoil

n: No cutting oneself for the dead or tattooing. The body was to be honored as God’s creation, not marked for pagan rites.

f.w: cuttings in your flesh for the dead

f.g: Tattoos or marked incisions.

n: Fathers must never force daughters into prostitution—a practice linked to some pagan temples—or the land would fill with wickedness.
Keep the Sabbaths and reverence the sanctuary—holy time and holy space.
Do not consult mediums or spiritists. Seeking guidance from the dead or the occult defiles God’s people.

f.g: Spirits supposedly contacted by mediums.
Wizards = those claiming secret knowledge; sorcerers.

n: Stand up in the presence of the elderly and honor them. Respect for age is tied to reverence for God.

f.g: Gray-haired head; an old person.

n: Do not mistreat foreigners living among you.

f.g: vex = oppress, mistreat

n: Foreigners are to be treated like native-born Israelites and loved as oneself. Israel knew from Egypt what it felt like to be a stranger.

f.w: thou shalt love him as thyself

n: Honesty in business: no cheating with measuring tools of any kind.

f.g: A measuring stick for length.

n: Scales, weights, and dry and liquid measures must be accurate. The God who freed Israel from Egypt expects honest dealing.

f.g: A dry measure, roughly a bushel or a bit less.
A liquid measure, about a gallon (3–4 liters).

n: A closing call to obey all God’s statutes. The refrain “I am the LORD” appears again and again in this chapter, grounding every command in who God is.
